passage: In the small-town school, Master-ji tapped his cane. "Hrithik, take Jomon's slate and lock it in the almirah. He talks too much." Hrithik stood up at once. Jomon's face crumpled, but Hrithik did not look at him. Meena at the back frowned, and two boys stared at the floor. Hrithik's stomach felt odd, as if a stone had settled there. But Master-ji had said it, and Master-ji was never wrong. He put the slate in the almirah and went back to his seat, holding the key very carefully.

qa.q: What did Master-ji tell Hrithik to do with Jomon's slate?
qa.a: Master-ji told Hrithik to take Jomon's slate and lock it in the almirah.

qa.q: Why does Hrithik obey even though Hrithik's stomach feels odd?
qa.a: Hrithik trusts Master-ji and believes Master-ji is never wrong; the stone-like feeling suggests an uneasy sense that the order may be unfair.

qa.q: What could Hrithik try at the moment the order is given?
qa.a: Hrithik could ask politely why, or say that Jomon needs the slate for the lesson, separating respect for the teacher from agreeing with every order.

qa.q: How might Jomon experience the order?
qa.a: Jomon's crumpled face suggests hurt and humiliation, made sharper by Hrithik taking the slate without looking at Jomon.

grounding: A child does what a teacher says only because of who said it, and cannot yet separate a fair rule from an unfair order.

passage: In a Toronto school library, Mr Grant told Class 4, "Nobody sits on the red carpet." The carpet was empty and soft. Yara raised her hand. "Why not, sir?" "Because I said so." Yara shrugged and sat on a chair. Fatima had a tired leg and looked longingly at the carpet, but she stood by the shelf for the whole story hour, reading spines. Two other children leaned against the wall. When the bell rang, Fatima's leg ached, but she said nothing, and neither did anyone else.

qa.q: Where did Fatima stand during story hour?
qa.a: Fatima stood by the shelf for the whole story hour, reading spines.

qa.q: Why does Fatima stand by the shelf despite a tired leg?
qa.a: Fatima follows the rule simply because the teacher said it and feels shy about asking; trust in adults is there, but the line between a fair rule and an unexplained one is not yet clear.

qa.q: What could Fatima do next time when a rule seems pointless and a leg is tired?
qa.a: Fatima could ask politely as Yara did, or say the leg is tired and ask whether sitting on a chair is allowed.

qa.q: What might Yara have been thinking when asking "Why not, sir?" and hearing "Because I said so"?
qa.a: Yara wanted a reason and was not convinced; shrugging and sitting on a chair suggests Yara accepted the rule without pretending it had been explained.

grounding: A child obeys a teacher's order without understanding it, showing healthy trust that has not yet learned to tell fair rules from unfair ones.

passage:
Uday, come, I'll tell you something from my schooldays. I'm your Zubin kaka, and I was a very obedient boy.
In Class 4, our teacher Mr Pestonji said, “Zubin, Behram came late again. Take his tiffin to the staffroom. No lunch for latecomers.” I didn't think. I walked to Behram's desk and took his steel tiffin while he looked at me.
Mr Pestonji also told us to wash hands before lunch and not run on the stairs. To me, it was all the same. A teacher said it, so it was right.
At lunch Behram sat with nothing. My own rice tasted like paper. I didn't know why yet. Years later I understood: some rules keep you safe, and some orders just hurt someone.

qa.q: What did Mr Pestonji tell young Zubin to take to the staffroom?
qa.a: He told him to take Behram's tiffin to the staffroom.

qa.q: How did young Zubin feel at lunch, even though he didn't know why?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and guilty; his own rice tasted like paper while Behram sat with nothing.

qa.q: At what point in the story could young Zubin have made a different choice?
qa.a: When the teacher gave the order, he could have asked why, or later quietly shared his lunch with Behram.

qa.q: How might Behram have felt when Zubin took his tiffin?
qa.a: He likely felt hurt and humiliated, and perhaps betrayed by a classmate simply doing as told.

grounding: An elder recalls obeying a teacher's unfair order simply because a teacher gave it, unable yet to tell a fair rule from an unfair one.

passage:
Rain had turned the school ground to mud, and the relay heats had to finish before the next shower. Ramesh sir blew his whistle. “No umbrellas on the track! Line up fast!”
Kavitha lined up at once. Rules were rules.
Then sir said, “Kavitha, go and tell Divya she's out. She's too slow for the team.”
Kavitha ran through the drizzle to Divya, who was tying her laces. “Sir says you're out. You're too slow.”
Divya's face crumpled. The other girls went quiet.
Kavitha ran back to her place. She had done both things sir asked, just the same way. But while she waited for the gun, she kept looking at Divya under the tree, and her chest felt heavy.

qa.q: What did Ramesh sir say about umbrellas?
qa.a: He said, "No umbrellas on the track!"

qa.q: What was Kavitha feeling as she looked at Divya under the tree?
qa.a: Her chest felt heavy, which shows she felt uneasy and guilty, though she didn't yet see why the order was different from the other rules.

qa.q: What could Kavitha have said when sir gave her the message?
qa.a: She could have asked sir to tell Divya himself, kindly, because some messages aren't a runner's job.

qa.q: How might the other girls have felt when Divya's face crumpled?
qa.a: They went quiet, so they probably felt awkward and sorry for Divya, and maybe worried it could happen to them.

grounding: Shows a child carrying out a coach's hurtful order just as readily as a fair rule, because of who gave it, amid rain and time pressure.

passage:
Dilnaz always listened to Lavanya aunty from the flat upstairs. Lavanya aunty was kind and gave the best laddoos in the building.
“Wash your hands before you eat, beta,” Lavanya aunty said on Monday. Dilnaz washed them twice.
“Don't play with the watchman's son,” she said on Tuesday, as Dilnaz came down with her cycle. “Play with Riddhi and Sameer.”
So when Bablu waved from the gate, Dilnaz rode past him, eyes forward. Riddhi and Sameer were busy anyway. She cycled alone in circles.
At home her mother asked why she wasn't playing with Bablu any more. “Lavanya aunty said,” Dilnaz answered, as if that explained everything. Her mother went very quiet.

qa.q: Who did Lavanya aunty tell Dilnaz to play with?
qa.a: She told her to play with Riddhi and Sameer.

qa.q: What does Dilnaz riding past Bablu with eyes forward suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: She seems a little uncomfortable, avoiding his eyes, but she trusts Lavanya aunty so much that she follows the order anyway.

qa.q: How could Dilnaz's mother talk with her about the two instructions?
qa.a: She could calmly ask why Dilnaz thinks aunty said it and explain that washing hands keeps you safe, but choosing friends by someone's job is unfair.

qa.q: How might Bablu feel when Dilnaz rode past him?
qa.a: He likely felt confused and hurt, not knowing why his friend suddenly ignored him.

grounding: Shows a child following an elder's unfair order just as she follows a fair rule, simply because of who said it.

passage:
"Ritu, put that book back. Sir said nobody touches the class library without asking me."
"I'm returning it, Pankaj."
"Still. Sir said."
Thomas looked up from his drawing. "And why can't Meena come out for the game?"
"Sir said anyone who forgot homework stays in at break."
"But her pencil box got stolen yesterday. That's why she couldn't do it."
Pankaj frowned. "Sir is Sir. He knows."
"Does he know about the pencil box?"
"...I don't know." Pankaj glanced at Meena, sitting alone with her head on the desk. "He said it, so it's the rule."
Ritu slid the book onto the shelf anyway. "The book rule is about books. This one's about a person."
Pankaj twisted the monitor badge on his shirt and said nothing.

qa.q: Why couldn't Meena do her homework, according to Thomas?
qa.a: Her pencil box got stolen yesterday.

qa.q: What does Pankaj twisting the monitor badge suggest?
qa.a: Pankaj seems uneasy and confused, torn between trusting Sir completely and a new doubt that the break rule is unfair to Meena.

qa.q: What could Pankaj do instead of repeating "Sir said"?
qa.a: Pankaj could tell Sir about the stolen pencil box and ask whether Meena can play; asking is still respectful.

qa.q: What is break time like for Meena?
qa.a: Meena sits alone with her head on the desk, likely feeling sad and left out for something that was not really her fault.

grounding: Shows a child who follows a teacher's orders simply because the teacher gave them, not yet separating a fair rule from an unfair one.
